summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on early-response (TTFT) and streaming microburst behavior. Action items assigned and next ops meeting for VPC routing scheduled.
transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-02-02
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Sofia M (Redwood AE), Ethan C (Redwood SE), Jamal P (Redwood SE), Priya R (Aquila ML), Marcus L (Aquila Infra), Diane O (Product), Toby (QA)

[00:00] Sofia: alright everyone thanks for joining, this is the EdgeBurst pilot weekly huddle. quick check-in on the microburst numbers and ttft. Ethan do you want to kick us off with a 2-min recap of the bench?

[00:22] Ethan: yeah sure, so last week we ran the 2 configs: baseline streaming with default kernel set and then hedged request path with batch size clamp 1 and conservative kv cache TTL. baseline median TTFT was about 120 ms, 95th hit 280 ms; hedged path got median down to 85 ms but 95th still floaty around 210. caveat we saw a high variance when the seqlen distribution skewed right in the customer traces.

[01:07] Priya: just to add, our real traffic has a long tail; maybe 20% of requests are > 1k tokens because of document context we're pulling in. we trimmed for the bench to under 512 but that doesn't reflect prod.

[01:25] Jamal: right, and that matters because kernel selection changes with seqlen. some of the smaller MLP kernels and the fused-attention path are faster up to 512 but once you cross that boundary the memory access pattern flips and you hit a different kernel set.

[01:58] Marcus: can you translate that into what we should expect for ttft variance? we care about p50/ p95 for the user flows, not just median.

[02:12] Ethan: practically, if your request seqlen distribution has 15-25% long tails, you'll see p95 degrade by ~30-40% versus a 90%<512 distribution. also microbursts—when many long requests land concurrently—cause io / kernel contention that increases TTFB.

[02:43] Diane: so is that more infra (IO contention) or model (kv cache warm/cold)?

[02:50] Jamal: both. KV cache cold starts matter for the first token if the cache hasn't been populated or if the routing sends you to a new replica. kernel contention is more of the throughput-layer problem, esp when our scheduler tries to batch dissimilar sequence lengths.

[03:16] Toby: quick note: our QA saw a spike in error 503s when we hit a synthetic microburst of 120 rps with 30% long seqlen. logs attached in the drive.

[03:32] Priya: ok, we should look at trimming context or prioritize the prefix heuristics; sometimes older context is low-value. but we can't just chop arbitrarily, product will push back if accuracy drops.

[03:50] Sofia: understood. proposal from Redwood is two tracks: (1) infra/runtime: adjust kernel candidate selection to prefer the low-latency fused kernels for <512, and pick a different kernel set once seqlen > 512 but with pre-warming heuristics; (2) request-side: hedging and early-response policy — i.e., stream partial output earlier and hedge to a second replica if ttft threshold exceeded.

[04:22] Marcus: hedging worries me because of cost. if we double requests, we double token and compute costs. we need a clear budget trade-off.

[04:35] Ethan: agreed, which is why hedging is targeted: we only hedge after X ms (we suggested 90 ms) and only for requests that match a short-answer affinity. we also suggested a dynamic hedging budget (e.g., cap to 5% of total QPS).

[04:58] Diane: can you show the numbers? what's the expected cost delta for 5% hedging on our 50 rps baseline?

[05:08] Sofia: quick back-of-envelope: 50 rps steady, 5% hedged => 2.5 extra calls/sec, multiply by average tokens per request we saw (approx 60 tokens) and Redwood unit pricing model gives you ~ +X% monthly — we'll send a spreadsheet with precise numbers.

[05:31] Priya: another variable is the quantization profile, we tested q4_0 in stage and saw some small quality regression on named entity extraction. want to avoid degrading clinical entity recall.

[05:45] Jamal: noted — kernel x quantization interplay is non-linear. some low-bit kernels have lower latency but can increase iteration count or force fallback which hurts ttft. We propose keeping q8_profile for sensitive flows and q4 for low-risk helper prompts.

[06:10] Marcus: can Redwood expose metric tags so we can break down cost/latency per prompt-type? we need to tie tradeoffs to product SLAs.

[06:20] Ethan: yes, Console can segregate by route and model variant; we'll add a pilot dashboard with token-level cost and per-route p50/p95.

[06:33] Diane: earlier you mentioned pre-warming on kernel flip; how does that work across replicas in our dedicated pool?

[06:41] Jamal: pre-warm is basically executing a short synthetic request to populate KV cache and warm the kernels when we detect a shift in sequence length mix. on dedicated pools we can schedule these warmups on idle cycles; cost is minimal compared to hedging. but if the pool is saturated pre-warms may compete.

[07:10] Priya: is there any risk with VPC egress that will slow down pre-warm network calls? our infra has strict egress rules.

[07:19] Marcus: yes we also have a NAT gateway constraint and occasional burst egress charges. we need to confirm VPC routing for Redwood-managed control plane calls.

[07:30] Sofia: ok we will add an ops sync item for VPC routing details — Marcus we'll need access to a network flow diagram and egress rules.

[07:42] Marcus: I'll put that in the ticket.

[07:47] Ethan: back to tuning: for this week we propose three experiments: A) tweak kernel selection thresholds so <400 uses fused-opt, 400-800 uses mid path, >800 uses shard-friendly kernels; B) enable hedging with 90 ms threshold capped at 5% QPS; C) implement lightweight prefix-trim based on token-value heuristic (Priya to define token-value).

[08:20] Priya: I'll work on the token-value heuristic and share sample rules. prefer not to remove clinical context. maybe we prefer to trim user history first.

[08:31] Diane: timeline? when can we see A/B numbers?

[08:35] Ethan: we can push kernel-candidate changes to the pilot cluster in 48 hours and run a 10k sample bench that afternoon; expect preliminary TTFT numbers in 72 hours.

[08:47] Sofia: great. also note we saw an odd outlier in last week's bench — one replica had p95>600ms inconsistent with others. Jamal did some trace analysis, any quick findings?

[08:58] Jamal: yes that was a scheduling jitter combined with a garbage collection pause on that runtime. GC was from a third-party collector in the telemetry stack, fixed by bumping the lib and isolating the telemetry thread. we rolled a hotfix.

[09:14] Marcus: thanks — that explains a lot of the noise.

[09:19] Toby: QA will re-run synthetic microbursts after changes, leaning on the 120 rps scenario and the 30% long-tail. we'll attach pass/fail criteria.

[09:30] Priya: quick product question — can we stream partial answers to the UI and then patch with final tokens? that's a front-end change but maybe helps perceived latency.

[09:38] Ethan: yes streaming partial payload is supported; Redwood runtime marks partial responses and then final chunk. the cost is negligible; UX gains are usually significant for perceived TTFT.

[09:50] Diane: ok we'll take that to the front-end team, maybe do A/B on perceived latency vs accuracy.

[09:58] Sofia: recap then: Redwood will push kernel candidate change A in 48 hrs, run 10k bench, share bench CSV; Ethan will prepare kernel matrix doc; Jamal will confirm telemetry hotfix is stable; Priya will deliver trim heuristic and run sample traces; Marcus will share VPC flow and egress rules; Toby/Q A will validate microburst test.

[10:25] Marcus: one more ask — can you include a quick note on SOC2 and data residency for the pilot? legal asked.

[10:33] Sofia: yes we'll attach the SOC2 summary and region residency docs; Redwood supports KMS and customer-managed keys for the Private pilot.

[10:44] Diane: cool. competitor question — LuminaAI proposed a different hedging model where they preemptively route all short-form requests to their tiny instance. any thoughts?

[10:55] Jamal: that's similar to proactive routing; it's cheaper but brittle — it requires a very accurate classifier to avoid sending long context to the tiny instance. we prefer dynamic hedging because it's safer for accuracy.

[11:15] Priya: ok sounds reasonable.

[11:20] Sofia: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and the kernel candidate doc. next sync same time next week? 15:00 PST 2027-02-09.

[11:35] All: thanks, bye.

Notes and attachments referenced: bench/edgeburst-week1.csv (Redwood drive), microburst-synth.log (Aquila drive), SOC2-summary.pdf (Redwood), vpc-egress-diagram.png (Aquila).

Transcription artifacts: occasional misattribution (Ethan/Jamal), numbers rounded in discussion, some proper nouns slightly off (e.g., q4_0 pronounced as q four zero), filler words preserved.
